audit_scope.description: This batch covers EVM precompiled contracts (identity, ModExp), browser-based wallet interaction standards (EIP-5749, EIP-7896), and EVM transient storage opcodes (EIP-1153). All components are within the Execution Layer.

in_scope: EVM precompiled contracts (identity at 0x04, ModExp at 0x05)

misclassified_entities.reason: This is an internal EVM component (smart contract or EOA) invoking precompiled contracts. Not an external entity crossing trust boundaries.
This is an internal EVM component (contract/EOA) calling precompiles. While untrusted in terms of data content, it's not an external entity to the EVM system.
Internal EVM entity invoking ModExp precompile. Not an external boundary crossing.
This represents a threat model actor, not an actual external system component. DoS attacks would come through normal transaction submission channels.
This is a threat model variant of EXT-DAPP, not a separate external entity. DApps are the same component regardless of intent.

trusted_external_entities.name: Browser Wallet Extension (MetaMask, Coinbase Wallet, etc.)
trusted_external_entities.rationale: Browser extensions are installed by users but operate with elevated privileges in the browser context. They inject EIP-1193 provider objects into web pages via window.evmproviders (EIP-5749). While users typically trust their wallet extensions, from a security boundary perspective these are untrusted code injecting into the browser DOM. Malicious extensions could inject fake providers, phish users, or manipulate transaction data before signing. The trust model must treat these as untrusted inputs requiring validation of provider metadata (UUID format, icon data URI format, EIP-1193 interface compliance) and user awareness that displayed information originates from potentially untrusted extensions.

trusted_external_entities.name: End User (DApp/Wallet User)
trusted_external_entities.entry_point: User input events (wallet selection, transaction approval)
trusted_external_entities.rationale: End users interact with DApps and wallets through browser UI, making wallet selection choices and approving transactions. Users are untrusted from the system's perspective as they may be confused, socially engineered, or make errors. In EIP-5749, users select wallet providers from displayed options. In EIP-7896, users approve transactions based on decoded calldata which may be misleading if the DApp provides false ABI specifications. The system must not assume users will detect malicious behavior and should provide clear security indicators and warnings.

trusted_external_entities.name: Decentralized Application (DApp)
trusted_external_entities.entry_point: EIP-1193 provider requests (wallet_sendCalls with interfaces capability)
trusted_external_entities.rationale: DApps are web applications that interact with wallets via standardized APIs like EIP-1193. In EIP-7896, DApps provide ABI specifications via the 'interfaces' capability in wallet_sendCalls requests, ostensibly to help wallets decode transaction calldata for user display. However, DApps are fundamentally untrusted - they could be malicious phishing sites providing false ABI specifications to mislead users about what transactions actually do. The EIP-7896 security section explicitly states 'Needs discussion' and acknowledges that malicious DApps could provide misleading ABIs. Wallets must treat all DApp-provided data as untrusted, validate ABI specifications against trusted databases when possible, and clearly indicate to users when ABI sources are not verified.

trusted_external_entities.name: External Trusted ABI Database (4byte.directory, Sourcify, Etherscan)
trusted_external_entities.rationale: External ABI databases provide verified contract interface specifications that wallets can use to validate DApp-provided ABIs. Services like 4byte.directory, Sourcify, and Etherscan are semi-trusted because: (1) they are operated by reputable community entities, (2) they use verification mechanisms like source code compilation matching, (3) they serve as independent third parties that don't benefit from misleading users. However, they are not fully trusted because they could be compromised, provide outdated data, experience availability issues, or contain incorrect entries. The communication channel (HTTPS) provides transport security but the data itself requires validation. Wallets should use these as verification sources but not as the sole basis for trust decisions.

boundary_edges.security_assumption: Browser extension content scripts can inject JavaScript objects into page context. The security model assumes: (1) Extensions are reviewed by browser vendors before installation, (2) Users intentionally install wallet extensions, (3) The browser's extension isolation prevents direct DOM manipulation by malicious pages, (4) DApps will validate provider metadata format (UUID, icon data URI) and EIP-1193 interface compliance. Threat: Malicious extensions could inject fake providers with misleading icons/names to phish users.

boundary_edges.target_component_interface: Wallet provider selection UI and transaction approval dialogs
boundary_edges.security_assumption: Users can distinguish between legitimate and malicious wallet providers based on displayed metadata (name, icon, UUID). Users can understand decoded transaction calldata sufficiently to make informed approval decisions. Threat: Users may be confused by similar-looking provider icons, misleading ABI decodings, or social engineering attacks. The system assumes users will read and understand security warnings, but user studies show this is often not the case.

DApps provide ABI specifications to help wallets decode transaction calldata for user transparency. The security model assumes wallets will: (1) Validate ABI specification format (version: abi-v1/abi-v2), (2) Perform case-sensitive address matching between interface addresses and call targets, (3) Optionally validate against trusted ABI databases, (4) Clearly indicate to users when ABIs are not verified. Critical threat: Malicious DApps can provide false ABI specifications that decode calldata to appear benign while actually performing malicious operations (e.g., showing 'transfer 1 token' while actually calling 'transferOwnership'). The EIP-7896 spec acknowledges this with 'Security Considerations: Needs discussion'.

Wallet extensions provide base64-encoded SVG icons for display in DApp wallet selection UIs. The security model assumes DApps will render SVGs using tags rather than inline SVG to prevent XSS attacks. Threat: Malicious extensions could embed JavaScript in SVG data. If DApps render inline SVG without sanitization, this enables XSS. The mitigation is to use tag rendering which prevents script execution. EIP-5749 explicitly recommends this approach.

boundary_edges.target_component_interface: HTTPS API for ABI verification queries
boundary_edges.security_assumption: External ABI databases (4byte.directory, Sourcify, Etherscan) provide verified contract interface data via HTTPS APIs. The security model assumes: (1) HTTPS provides transport security and authenticity, (2) Database operators maintain accurate verified data, (3) Source code verification mechanisms (compilation matching) correctly validate ABIs, (4) Databases have sufficient uptime for availability. Threats: (a) HTTPS compromise or MITM attacks could provide false data, (b) Database compromise could inject malicious ABIs, (c) Availability issues could prevent verification, (d) Verification logic bugs could approve incorrect ABIs. Wallets should cache verified ABIs, handle failures gracefully, and consider database reputation when making trust decisions.

notes: All 4 truly external entities have been modeled with boundary edges.
5 entities were identified as misclassified (internal EVM components or threat actors rather than external systems).
EIP-1153 (Transient Storage) contains no external entities - it defines internal EVM opcodes operating entirely within the execution context.
The primary security concerns in this batch relate to browser-based wallet interactions where untrusted DApps and extensions interact with users through browser DOM and API calls.
EIP-7896 has an acknowledged security gap in its specification (Security Considerations: Needs discussion) regarding trust in DApp-provided ABIs.
All boundary edges involve untrusted or semi-trusted external entities requiring validation and user awareness.
